newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Frozen bonds clouding Russia Eurobond debut.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Frozen bonds clouding Russia Eurobond debut.

text.p: Russia's plans to return to international capital markets for the first time since the 1917 revolution were overshadowed on Monday by news a scandal involving domestic bonds was much bigger than had been thought.
Figures released by Russian police showed the authorities had seized $74 million of dollar-denominated MinFin bonds this year, not $24 million as previously reported.
A Russian police detective told Reuters his local prosecutor's office had ordered $56.81 million of the MinFin domestic dollar bonds to be frozen in June.
Mikhail Ignatyev, a detective with the fifth central Moscow police precinct, said the bonds had been frozen as part of an investigation into a small bank which has since been closed.
The finance ministry had already issued a list in July of $24.22 million bonds which had been frozen, some of which had been stolen in the breakaway republic of Chechnya.
Because some $6.93 million worth of bonds are on both lists, the total now known to have been seized by the authorities comes to $74 million.

News of the latest freezing had little impact on prices of the bonds, usually traded actively in Russia and abroad, because trading had mostly dried up since rumours about the freezing began to circulate last week.
But the news cast a shadow over Russia's plans to issue its first Eurobond this month.
A senior finance ministry official, commenting on rumours in Russian markets that the bond would be postponed, said it would go ahead by the end of the month.
"We are going to do it in November," Vladimir Dmitriyev, deputy head of the foreign credits department, told Reuters.
Russian officials will start a two-week roadshow, or series of presentations in major financial centres, in Tokyo on November 11 to raise investor interest in the issue.

The issue, whose size has not yet been set but which bankers expect to be for around $300-500 million, will bring much needed dollars to Russia's cash-strapped government and mark Russia's return to financial respectability. The return was expected to open the way for further foreign investment.
But potential investors could now be put off by the MinFin scandal, financial analysts in Moscow said.
Holders of the bearer securities said if they bought the bonds in good faith, they should not be penalised if their bonds turned out to have been stolen earlier.
Indeed, Russia's Civil Code expressly protects holders of bearer securities from seizures of this kind.
And syndication managers for the Eurobond can put a positive spin on the matter, Renaissance Capital said.

They are likely to point out that the Eurobonds, unlike MinFins, are issued under international not Russian law and placed in the international Euroclear custody, rather than in Russian banks, the Moscow investment bank said.
"However, this recent freezing episode serves to highlight the still evolving nature of Russian financial legislation for potential Eurobond investors," it said in a research paper.
The first wave of freezing, confirmed in July, hit prices in June when the speculation surfaced. But prices have generally risen most of the year on optimism about the Eurobond.
The finance ministry has stopped servicing the frozen bonds but has not been able to resolve the issue with the judicial authorities.
Neither the finance ministry nor Vneshtorgbank, the main depositary for the bonds, has commented on the latest freezing news despite the uncertainty generated by last week's rumours.

Although the order to freeze the $56.81 million was issued in June, an official at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Moscow said the bank had been advised by the depositary only last week that bonds on the June list had been frozen.
